item.title: FinancialJuice: Bank of America: Long-End Yield Pressure Remains the Key Risk for Markets - FJElite
item.description:
The 30-year US Treasury is heading for a sixth consecutive year of negative price returns, the longest such streak since 1963-69. Despite sharp declines across risk assets, long-end yields remain close to recent highs, reinforcing the concern that there may be no easy Q4 “release valve” through lower rates. The bigger structural risk is that, in the next downturn, yields rise rather than fall because debt levels are too high.

The key question is whether Fed tightening ends before recession risks become dominant. If weaker credit and equities force the Fed to stop, markets could begin positioning for peak rates by March or April. The clearest signs would likely come through a weaker dollar and stabilisation in assets already hit hardest by tightening, such as crypto, gold and Korean equities.

A soft landing would leave sub-7,000 S&P levels looking more attractive and could eventually support a spring rebound in cyclicals, chips, copper, crypto and consumer names once the narrative shifts from hikes to cuts. The harder-landing risk is that GDP and earnings expectations are cut further and the AI capex/K-shaped wealth “boom loop” reverses into a broader “doom loop,” forcing investors to sell crowded defensive and low-volatility positions as well.

item.title: FinancialJuice: Citigroup: Walmart Results Point to Resilient Spending but More Value-Conscious Consumers - FJElite
item.description:
Strong Walmart earnings reinforce the resilience of the US consumer after solid October retail sales, but the details suggest spending behaviour is becoming more selective. Share gains were led by households earning more than $100,000, indicating that even higher-income consumers are increasingly seeking value. Management also noted some pressure from higher fuel prices, although overall spending remains reasonably strong.

The picture remains consistent with a more K-shaped consumer backdrop: higher-income households are still spending but becoming more price-conscious, while lower-income consumers remain more exposed to fuel, transport and essential costs. Walmart’s guidance was broadly in line, and elevated valuation may limit enthusiasm despite the solid print. Consumer staples still look relatively well supported into the holiday season, while recent “preparedness shopping” in items such as propane, bottled water and camping gear appears to have pulled some demand forward.

item.title: FinancialJuice: Goldman Sachs: AI/China Restrictions Add to Broader Pressure on Tech Valuations - FJElite
item.description:
Markets sold off sharply from the US open despite what had initially looked like supportive catalysts, with a mix of macro and micro concerns driving a violent liquidation. The most immediate pressure appears to be the US move toward a much stricter chip-export regime. New BIS rules tighten restrictions not only on direct advanced-chip sales to China, but also on Chinese access to advanced compute through overseas data centres and on the use of foreign foundries for leading-edge production. The near-term risk is less about permanently losing Chinese demand and more about uncertainty over licensing and access, which could freeze incremental investment decisions.

That uncertainty is adding to weakness across Asian data-centre names, broader Chinese equities and potentially commodities such as copper and gold, though positioning and liquidity are also playing a role. More broadly, the latest rules compound existing concerns already weighing on AI multiples: a higher cost of capital, tighter data-centre restrictions, possible oversupply and efficiency gains in inference, and insufficient revenue growth to justify the scale of capex.

item.title: FinancialJuice: Credit Ágricole: FX Weekly - FJElite
item.description:
The AI trade has been battered by the Democrat blue wave, concerns about Nvidia’s corporate leadership and the US’s new restrictions on access to advanced chips physically as well as via remote access. Despite US technology stocks being weaker, the USD remains dominant. We hold to the view that the unwinding of the AI trade is bad news for the USD. Much of the currency’s attraction in 2026 has been in investing in US technology stocks rather than USTs. People could argue that the recent price action suggests the USD's safe-haven-with-yield status has returned.

Weakening risk sentiment is a significant positive for the USD vs the CAD, GBP, AUD, NZD, NOK and JPY. It is not important for the USD’s performance vs the EUR, CHF or SEK. Importantly, risk sentiment is a bigger driver than rates for only GBP/USD and is equally important to rates for AUD/USD. So the jump in US rates is behind most of the USD's recent strength rather than a run to the currency as a safe haven. Sovereign risk remains more important than general risk for EUR/USD and USD/SEK. For USD/JPY, sovereign risk is a bigger driver than general risk sentiment, but rates are the largest driver of the exchange rate.

This matters for the coming week as economic performance and inflation will be compared across G10 currencies. The US, UK and Eurozone see the releases of PMI as well German IFO and US consumer confidence data. French and Spanish inflation data will be compared with US core PCE data. Australian inflation could remain stubborn which could risk whipsawing investors after weak labour market data.

The near-term outlook of the broad USD across the board could continue to follow the predictions of the ‘USD smile’ and thus take its cue from the resilience of market risk sentiment and the price action in US rate markets. FX investors will also scrutinise the performance of the US stocks in the wake of Anthropic’s IPO [Crédit Agricole CIB is acting as joint bookrunner]. They would be looking for any evidence that the IPO could revive market appetite for the beleaguered US tech stocks, in particular. Any ‘buy-the-rumour-sell-the-fact’ equity price action could eventually hurt the USD appeal, in our view.

item.title: FinancialJuice: Deutsche Bank: Chips and the USD - FJElite
item.description:
What do chips have to do with a new era of dollar dominance? As we discuss in this paper - a great deal. Chips are not only critical to the future of AI but have recently emerged as a huge driver of global trade and capital flows.

It is well known that the US is dominant in upstream chip technology and downstream compute. This note delves deeper into the workings of the middle of the chain where flows have been reinforcing the dollar's global role. The manufacturing of chips largely takes place in Asia where chip-related trade surpluses have ballooned. As we show, these surpluses are finding their way back to the US via investments in US capital markets. Asian chip surpluses are not being recycled into US Treasuries like petrodollar surpluses were, but into US equities. Foreign inflows into US equities have crossed USDItn a year and become the mainstay of US deficit funding. The biggest source of increase over the past year has come from Asia.

Equity flows have not just been supporting the US dollar but have provided financing to the companies driving the AI buildout and chips boom itself. This introduces forms of circularity and potential instability to global flows. Moreover, equities are a much riskier asset class than bonds - US stocks are three times as volatile as Treasuries, with tech stocks up to ten times as much. Growing dollar dependence on inherently riskier capital should spill into higher US dollar volatility over time. The rise of chips as a driver of dollar dominance can be seen as a symptom of change in the ultimate source of US power - from geopolitical to technological leadership. This power is increasingly concentrated in the private sector with dollar supportive flows intermediated via private balance sheets.

Understanding this new framework and its risks is even more important given rapid shifts in news flow around AI, from the US political climate, high-stakes capital market raisings, potential tightening in export controls, and the highly consequential technology race with China.
